questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $2\,m$ when its velocity is $8\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/017463f3ac8abac9c2b00c4d9a715a4109a5f4bc1b070e0a12c4d3a7bac64351.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=2\,\text{m}$ when $v=8\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =2(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =32-8 \\ C & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+24 \\ {v}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+48 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}+12) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=(4-2x)\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/7bd0200a651aec7283e5c96d3cdc1589d795531e179ca0eb7cc36ef5bad8de56.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=4-2x.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4-2x.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4-2x \\ \frac{1}{4-2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{4-2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{4-2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x| & =t+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|2-x| & =-2t-2K \\ 2-x & =C{e}^{-2t} \\ x & =2-C{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=2-2{e}^{-2t}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)={e}^{-2x}\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/8faba5a783797f7025f51ec1ae587cb68355dff7138278689346c2f713275562.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)={e}^{-2x}.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}={e}^{-2x}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & ={e}^{-2x} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{-2x}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int {e}^{2x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x} & =t+K \\ {e}^{2x} & =2t+C \\ 2x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+C) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1).
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(4{x}^{3}+4x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=2\,\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/4e0b8b816ca3b86fa90ea785df1308f53a4763baa2c2aa2192b9d7bfa0259855.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4{x}^{3}+4x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4{x}^{3}+4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}+4x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{6})^{2} & ={1}^{4}+2(1)^{2}+C \\ 3 & =3+C \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{2({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({2}^{4}+2(2)^{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{48} \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+\frac{x}{2}){m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=5\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=2\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108748/assets/d9482b116bad201dec2c71f173bf18d7dc2f170acbb37052151bba38a7898450.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+\frac{x}{2}){m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+\frac{x}{2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+\frac{x}{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int (2+\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=5\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(5)^{2} & =2(0)+\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+C \\ \frac{25}{2} & =0+0+C \\ C & =\frac{25}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{25}{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4x+25 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4x+25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4x+25}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=2$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+4(2)+25} \\  & =\sqrt{2+8+25} \\  & =\sqrt{35} \\  & ≈5.9\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.
